Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Fabrication Toolkit for Kicad PCBWay Fabrication Toolkit for Kicad by: PCBWay Oct 11,2023 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Recently, PCBWay added a plug-in called PCBWay Fabrication Toolkit to Kicad: With just one click of the mouse, four files can be exported from the layout file automatically: Gerber file, IPC-Netlist file, BOM file and Pick and Place file, which can significantly improves the efficiency of pre-production work. Installation from the Official KiCad Repositories After installation, the plugin will appear on the right side of the navigation bar. And users can use it to export all the production files with just a click. Process demonstration： Sending the files to PCBWay, and they can be used for production after being reviewed by the staff. Note: If you want to place an assembly order, please be sure to add MPN information to the BOM. This can help the quoter source the devices you need more accurately. Manual installation Except for the way mentioned before, you can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Fabrication-Toolkit-for-KiCad: Open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About BOM Through BOM files, we can get all information of the components used in your design. In order to speed up the quotation process, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) If you have more suggestions, please leave a message below, PCBWay has committed to providing everyone with high-quality services. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad by: Anson Apr 01,2022 Posted in News Kicad PCB design Send your layout to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. Have you ever thought that when you complete the design on KiCad, you can place an order on pcbway with just one click? Now this idea is finally achieved (it's not an April Fool's joke). When you click PCBWay Plug-in button on Kicad, we will export these files in your project ( Please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin released at 2026 )： 1.Gerber files in correct format for production 2.IPC-Netlist file 3.Bom-file that includes all information of components 4.Pick and Place-file used in assembly You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files( usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before the production. Note:We have updated plugin for Kicad 10,you could also place assembly order directly now. But we need to get the component "Manufacture Part Number". Please confirm you run the "Update Board from Schematic" and install the latest version of the plugin. ﻿ Installation from the official KiCad repositories Just open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the KiCad main menu an install the "PCBWay Plug-in for KiCad" plugin from the selection list. Manual installation You can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Plug-in-for-Kicad , then open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About Bom We can get all information of components used in your design ( please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin) . In order to speed up the quotation of components, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) You just need to add the properties in your schematic like the picture shows: As a sponsor of KiCad, we will always support its development. Note: Thanks to the open source community. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad by: Anson Apr 01,2022 Posted in News Kicad PCB design Send your layout to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. Have you ever thought that when you complete the design on KiCad, you can place an order on pcbway with just one click? Now this idea is finally achieved (it's not an April Fool's joke). When you click PCBWay Plug-in button on Kicad, we will export these files in your project ( Please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin released at 2026 )： 1.Gerber files in correct format for production 2.IPC-Netlist file 3.Bom-file that includes all information of components 4.Pick and Place-file used in assembly You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files( usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before the production. Note:We have updated plugin for Kicad 10,you could also place assembly order directly now. But we need to get the component "Manufacture Part Number". Please confirm you run the "Update Board from Schematic" and install the latest version of the plugin. ﻿ Installation from the official KiCad repositories Just open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the KiCad main menu an install the "PCBWay Plug-in for KiCad" plugin from the selection list. Manual installation You can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Plug-in-for-Kicad , then open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About Bom We can get all information of components used in your design ( please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin) . In order to speed up the quotation of components, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) You just need to add the properties in your schematic like the picture shows: As a sponsor of KiCad, we will always support its development. Note: Thanks to the open source community. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay to Exhibit at SIDO Lyon 2026: Meet Us at Booth E122 PCBWay to Exhibit at SIDO Lyon 2026: Meet Us at Booth E122 by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News As smart technologies continue to transform industrial products and connected devices, reliable hardware manufacturing has become an essential part of turning innovative concepts into real-world products. From September 16 to 17, 2026, SIDO Lyon 2026 will bring together technology providers, industrial companies, startups, and innovation professionals at the Lyon Convention Centre in France. The event focuses on the convergence of IoT, Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, and Extended Reality (XR), with a strong emphasis on practical industrial applications and digital transformation. PCBWay will be exhibiting at Booth E122. We warmly invite you to visit us and explore how our manufacturing services can support your next hardware project. PCBWay at SIDO Lyon 2026 Event: SIDO Lyon 2026 Date: September 16–17, 2026 Venue: Lyon Convention Centre, Cité Internationale, Lyon, France Booth: E122 SIDO Lyon is designed to connect technology solutions with companies working on real-world digitalization and Industry 4.0 projects. The 2026 edition is expected to bring together more than 300 exhibitors, with technologies covering IoT, AI, robotics, digital twins, XR, cybersecurity, and prototyping. For hardware developers, these technologies ultimately depend on one critical foundation: reliable physical products that can move efficiently from concept to production. From Prototype to Production Developing an IoT device, robotic system, industrial controller, or smart product often involves more than designing a PCB. Hardware teams may need to coordinate electronics, mechanical components, enclosures, prototypes, and final assembly throughout the development process. PCBWay provides a range of manufacturing services to support these requirements, including: PCB Manufacturing PCB Assembly (PCBA) HDI and Flex PCB Rigid-Flex PCB CNC Machining 3D Printing Injection Molding Sheet Metal Fabrication Box Build Assembly This integrated approach helps hardware teams reduce the complexity of working with multiple manufacturing suppliers and makes it easier to move from an initial prototype toward small-batch and production manufacturing. Meet PCBWay at Booth E122 If you are attending SIDO Lyon 2026, come and visit PCBWay at Booth E122. The exhibition will be an opportunity to discuss your current or upcoming hardware projects, explore manufacturing solutions, and learn more about how PCBWay can support projects ranging from early-stage prototypes to production. Whether you are developing an IoT device, robotic system, industrial controller, smart sensor, embedded product, or other electronic hardware, our team will be happy to discuss your manufacturing requirements. Visit us at Booth E122 and let's bring your next hardware idea to life. Unlock Color PCB Printing with PCBWay! by: PCBWay Mar 08,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Color PCB Printing PCBWay Service Nowadays, traditional PCB printing technology can no longer meet the aesthetic requirements of modern circuit board production. To better fulfill customers' design needs, we are pleased to announce that PCBWay has introduced UV printing equipment. This equipment utilizes UV-curable inks to achieve high-quality image printing on various materials, including fiberglass boards, metal substrates, ceramic substrates, flexible boards, and rigid-flex boards. Entrance https://www.pcbway.com/orderonline.aspx Prerequisites for Ordering Maximum size for a single piece: 270*470MM; Selection of background soldermask color required. Design Specifications Drill holes, traces, soldermasks, and outline designs must comply with specifications. Avoid placing colored characters in areas with solder mask openings, such as surface-mount pads or through-hole pads. What kind of files should be provided for color printing? Method One : Draw colored characters on the silkscreen layer of the Gerber and provide reference pictures. For example: Method Two : If you include information about colored silkscreen in the Gerber layer, each individual color must have its own layer. If there is only one layer, we can only print one color. [This method is not recommended] . If you need to print in multiple colors, we recommend using method One and providing us with a reference picture. 4.Please send the images you want to print on the PCB in the following formats: AI, PDF, JPEG, PNG, TIFF, etc., and indicate your desired printing location on the board. 5.If the image contains a QR code, please ensure that the QR code can be accurately scanned and recognized. Note : If you choose UV printing Multi-color, we will use matte UV color printing by default. When designing the colored characters on the bottom layer, be careful not to design the colored characters as mirrored inverses. (The process of color printing is different from that of standard PCB silkscreen printing. When printing colorful characters on the bottom layer, they are printed with the bottom layer of the PCB facing up.) For situations where the entire top or bottom side requires full-color printing, regardless of the solder mask color you choose, we will use a white solder mask on the full-color printed side and then proceed with the color printing. This is for a better printing effect. Please upload the print image, positioning image, and Gerber in one compressed file. By providing a clear positioning image and necessary instructions, you can assist PCBWay in accurately determining and achieving the desired printing position. Matte UV Color Printing vs. Glossy UV Color Printing Matte ink does not increase the overall thickness, and the PCB's appearance looks smooth. Glossy ink increases the overall thickness and may affect the soldering of component pads. The appearance is beautiful but uneven. Features Adopting UV-LED lamp curing, which enables instant drying, can significantly enhances production efficiency. UV printing technology employs UV-curable inks, ensuring firm and clear printing information resistant to fading, thus enhancing product identification and aesthetics. The normal print survives SMT reflow. UV printing technology can present images in various colors and styles, meeting customers' personalized requirements. Professional industrial-grade UV printers support high-precision printing, delivering exquisite results whether on flat panels or rolled materials. Unlike traditional printing methods, UV printing does not produce volatile organic compounds during the production process, ensuring air quality in the production workshop and providing employees with a safer and healthier working environment. FAQ on UV Printing: Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with water? Yes, it can be cleaned with water. Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with alcohol? It is more difficult to clean after being exposed to alcohol and baked (currently, the board undergoes a short baking process after UV printing). However, with increased contact time with alcohol and vigorous scrubbing, it can be removed. This also depends on whether the UV is on the copper surface or the solder mask surface. How hard is the UV printed surface (sensitivity to scratches)? The UV surface is not sensitive to scratches. However, compared to the solder mask, it is less scratch-resistant because UV printing is ink that is sprayed on and is relatively thin. Welcome to give it a try if you're interested! Besides, PCBWay will continue to enhance its manufacturing capabilities to bring more choices and personalized services to customers in the future. Verify Now Blog > PCB Design Layout Guidelines for Routing PCB Design Layout Guidelines for Routing by: Mia Jul 17,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Design Guideline PCB Routing PCB Layout 1. Length Control in Routing Length controlling is very important in PCB design. The traces should be kept as short as possible to avoid introducing unnecessary interference due to excessive length. For important signal traces, such as clock signal traces, be sure to place its oscillator very close to the device. 2. Direction Control in Routing The routing directions of adjacent layers should be orthogonal to avoid the signal traces of adjacent layers running in the same direction, thus reducing unnecessary crosstalk between layers. 3. Rules for Chamfer Sharp angles and right angles should be avoided in PCB design, otherwise, unnecessary radiation will be generated and the process performance will be poor. 4. Open Loop Detection in Routing Generally, dangling lines are not allowed. This is mainly to avoid the "antenna effect" and reduce unnecessary interference radiation and reception. Otherwise, serious consequences may occur. 5. Try to Avoid Self-loop Routing When designing PCB, we should pay attention to the situation where signal traces form self-loops between different layers. Especially when routing multi-layer boards, signal traces are routed between layers, which has a greater chance of forming self-loops. Self-loops can cause radiation interference. 6. Rules for Ground Loop The minimal loop rule states that the loop area formed by a signal trace and its return path should be as small as possible. The smaller the loop area, the less external radiation it emits and the less interference it receives from the outside. 7. Rules for the Integrity of Power and Ground Layers For areas with dense vias, care should be taken to avoid the holes connecting to each other in the hollowed-out areas of the power and ground layers, which would segment the plane layer. This may destroy the integrity of the plane layer and further increase the loop area of ​​the signal trace in the ground layer. 8. 3W Rule In order to reduce crosstalk between traces, the trace spacing should be large enough. When the center-to-center distance between traces is at least three times the space width, 70% of the electric field will not interfere with each other, known as the 3W rule. To achieve 98% of the electric field not interfering with each other, a 10W spacing can be used. 9. Shielding Protection Shielding protection corresponds to the ground loop rule, which is actually to minimize the loop area of ​​the signal. It is more common in some important signals, such as clock signals and synchronization signals. For some particularly important, high-frequency signals, a coaxial cable shielding design should be considered. This involves isolating the signal traces with ground traces on all sides (top, bottom, left, and right). Additionally, careful consideration must be given to how effectively to connect the shield ground to the actual ground plane. 10. Rules for Impedance Matching Check The routing width in the same network should be kept consistent. Changes in trace width can cause non-uniform characteristic impedance of the circuit, leading to reflections when the transmission speed is high. This should be avoided in the design whenever possible. Under certain conditions, such as structures similar to lead-out traces of connectors or the lead-out traces of BGA packages, changes in trace width may be unavoidable, so the effective length of the inconsistent sections should be minimized. 11. Rules for Overlapping Power and Ground Layers Different power layers should avoid overlapping in space to reduce interference between different power supplies. This is especially important for power supplies with significantly different voltages. If it is difficult to avoid, consider placing a ground plane in between. 12. 20H Principle To prevent board edge radiation, the power plane should be retracted during design. Using H (the dielectric thickness between the power and ground) as a unit, a retraction of 20H can confine 70% of the electric field within the edge of the ground layer, while a retraction of 100H can confine 98% of the electric field within it. When the center-to-center distance between traces is at least three times the space width, 70% of the electric field will not interfere with each other, known as the 3W rule. To achieve 98% of the electric field not interfering with each other, a 10W spacing can be used. 9. Shielding Protection Shielding protection corresponds to the ground loop rule, which is actually to minimize the loop area of ​​the signal. It is more common in some important signals, such as clock signals and synchronization signals. For some particularly important, high-frequency signals, a coaxial cable shielding design should be considered. This involves isolating the signal traces with ground traces on all sides (top, bottom, left, and right). Additionally, careful consideration must be given to how effectively to connect the shield ground to the actual ground plane. 10. Rules for Impedance Matching Check The routing width in the same network should be kept consistent. Changes in trace width can cause non-uniform characteristic impedance of the circuit, leading to reflections when the transmission speed is high. This should be avoided in the design whenever possible. Under certain conditions, such as structures similar to lead-out traces of connectors or the lead-out traces of BGA packages, changes in trace width may be unavoidable, so the effective length of the inconsistent sections should be minimized. 11. Rules for Overlapping Power and Ground Layers Different power layers should avoid overlapping in space to reduce interference between different power supplies. This is especially important for power supplies with significantly different voltages. If it is difficult to avoid, consider placing a ground plane in between. 12. 20H Principle To prevent board edge radiation, the power plane should be retracted during design. Using H (the dielectric thickness between the power and ground) as a unit, a retraction of 20H can confine 70% of the electric field within the edge of the ground layer, while a retraction of 100H can confine 98% of the electric field within it. Verify Now Blog > HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design by: Mila Sep 03,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hdi pcb HDI pcb design optical module pcb high speed pcb layout An optical module PCB is a typical high-frequency, high-density HDI PCB precision board. Its material selection is closely related to transmission rate, link length, loss budget, and device platforms. While 10G and lower modules can use materials like high-Tg FR-4, high-speed modules operating at 25G, 56G, 100G, 400G, and 800G impose stringent requirements on low-loss materials, impedance control, and manufacturing consistency. Below are seven core layout design points and key differences compared to standard PCBs, focusing on high speed pcb layout and practical signal integrity engineering without rigid design fallacies. 1. Substrate Selection and StackUp Design Substrate selection and layer stackup form the foundation for stable high-frequency transmission, directly determining link insertion loss, impedance accuracy, and signal integrity. Multi-Dimensional Rate-Matched Selection: For 25G+ channels, select substrates considering Nyquist frequency, link length, insertion loss budget, dielectric loss, copper foil roughness, and stackup. For long-distance or low-loss channels, choose mid-to-low loss high-speed substrates. Non-critical areas like low-speed control and power can use high-Tg FR-4 to balance performance and cost on an optical module PCB. Adjacent Reference Ground Planes: High-speed differential signal layers should adopt a "signal-reference ground" structure to minimize edge-field coupling. Power layers should pair with adjacent ground layers to optimize PDN impedance via inter-layer capacitance. Pre-Simulation Impedance Modeling: Determine stackup parameters early through SI simulation. The industry standard target is typically 100 ohms differential impedance, with high-performance channels strictly controlling tolerances within +/- 5%. 2. High-Speed Differential TX/RX Signal Integrity High-speed differential signals are the core of data transmission in an optical module PCB. Design should focus on eliminating geometric discontinuities and parasitic interference. Symmetry and Equal Length: Match trace widths, spacing, bends, and via layouts for differential pairs. Advanced HDI pcb design requires controlling intra-pair length skew to prevent differential-to-common mode noise conversion. Trace Geometry Continuity: Use 45-degree angles or smooth arc transitions instead of rigid 90-degree turns. High-frequency reflections stem mostly from vias, pads, stubs, and split reference planes rather than standard trace corners. Minimal Via Structures and Stub Optimization: Minimize layer transitions. For long through-hole structures, apply back-drilling to remove residual stubs, cutting down reflections and resonances. （Backdrill + Via Stub） Unbroken High-Frequency Return Paths: Avoid routing differential traces across ground splits or slot gaps. Provide nearby stitching ground vias whenever signals switch layers. (Differential Pair + Reference Plane + Return Path) Crosstalk Mitigation: Apply the 3W rule during initial layout for proper spacing. For 112G PAM4 ultra-high-speed scenarios, refine trace spacing with 3D EM simulation and add ground via shielding walls where necessary. 3. Optoelectronic Isolation and Sensitive Layout Optical modules combine sensitive analog signals with high-speed digital logic. The analog front-end requires isolation from power and digital noise. Physical Isolation: Separate TOSA/ROSA components and TIA analog circuits from high-speed digital traces and switching power supplies based on form factors (SFP, QSFP, OSFP). Short Analog Traces: Keep weak analog traces from optical devices to TIA and driver ICs as short as possible, avoiding parallel routing alongside high-speed digital lines. Analog Circuit Shielding: Implement localized ground shielding or small metal shields around laser drivers and TIA circuits to isolate high-frequency digital noise. 4. Power Integrity (PI) Optimization Focus on low-impedance return paths, minimal current loops, and sub-region noise reduction. Minimal Loop Decoupling: Configure decoupling networks based on target PDN impedance. Place capacitors close to power pins to minimize parasitic inductance. Solid Ground Plane Priority: Maintain a continuous, low-impedance ground plane across the HDI PCB to provide a solid reference. Verify Now Blog > HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design by: Mila Sep 03,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hdi pcb HDI pcb design optical module pcb high speed pcb layout An optical module PCB is a typical high-frequency, high-density HDI PCB precision board. Its material selection is closely related to transmission rate, link length, loss budget, and device platforms. While 10G and lower modules can use materials like high-Tg FR-4, high-speed modules operating at 25G, 56G, 100G, 400G, and 800G impose stringent requirements on low-loss materials, impedance control, and manufacturing consistency. Below are seven core layout design points and key differences compared to standard PCBs, focusing on high speed pcb layout and practical signal integrity engineering without rigid design fallacies. 1. Substrate Selection and StackUp Design Substrate selection and layer stackup form the foundation for stable high-frequency transmission, directly determining link insertion loss, impedance accuracy, and signal integrity. Multi-Dimensional Rate-Matched Selection: For 25G+ channels, select substrates considering Nyquist frequency, link length, insertion loss budget, dielectric loss, copper foil roughness, and stackup. For long-distance or low-loss channels, choose mid-to-low loss high-speed substrates. Non-critical areas like low-speed control and power can use high-Tg FR-4 to balance performance and cost on an optical module PCB. Adjacent Reference Ground Planes: High-speed differential signal layers should adopt a "signal-reference ground" structure to minimize edge-field coupling. Power layers should pair with adjacent ground layers to optimize PDN impedance via inter-layer capacitance. Pre-Simulation Impedance Modeling: Determine stackup parameters early through SI simulation. The industry standard target is typically 100 ohms differential impedance, with high-performance channels strictly controlling tolerances within +/- 5%. 2. High-Speed Differential TX/RX Signal Integrity High-speed differential signals are the core of data transmission in an optical module PCB. Design should focus on eliminating geometric discontinuities and parasitic interference. Symmetry and Equal Length: Match trace widths, spacing, bends, and via layouts for differential pairs. Advanced HDI pcb design requires controlling intra-pair length skew to prevent differential-to-common mode noise conversion. Trace Geometry Continuity: Use 45-degree angles or smooth arc transitions instead of rigid 90-degree turns. High-frequency reflections stem mostly from vias, pads, stubs, and split reference planes rather than standard trace corners. Minimal Via Structures and Stub Optimization: Minimize layer transitions. For long through-hole structures, apply back-drilling to remove residual stubs, cutting down reflections and resonances. （Backdrill + Via Stub） Unbroken High-Frequency Return Paths: Avoid routing differential traces across ground splits or slot gaps. Provide nearby stitching ground vias whenever signals switch layers. (Differential Pair + Reference Plane + Return Path) Crosstalk Mitigation: Apply the 3W rule during initial layout for proper spacing. For 112G PAM4 ultra-high-speed scenarios, refine trace spacing with 3D EM simulation and add ground via shielding walls where necessary. 3. Optoelectronic Isolation and Sensitive Layout Optical modules combine sensitive analog signals with high-speed digital logic. The analog front-end requires isolation from power and digital noise. Physical Isolation: Separate TOSA/ROSA components and TIA analog circuits from high-speed digital traces and switching power supplies based on form factors (SFP, QSFP, OSFP). Short Analog Traces: Keep weak analog traces from optical devices to TIA and driver ICs as short as possible, avoiding parallel routing alongside high-speed digital lines. Analog Circuit Shielding: Implement localized ground shielding or small metal shields around laser drivers and TIA circuits to isolate high-frequency digital noise. 4. Power Integrity (PI) Optimization Focus on low-impedance return paths, minimal current loops, and sub-region noise reduction. Minimal Loop Decoupling: Configure decoupling networks based on target PDN impedance. Place capacitors close to power pins to minimize parasitic inductance. Solid Ground Plane Priority: Maintain a continuous, low-impedance ground plane across the HDI PCB to provide a solid reference. Apply localized filtering for sensitive analog zones rather than single-point star grounding across the board. Thermal Copper Pour for Power Chips: Place large copper areas with thermal via arrays beneath heat-generating components like laser drivers to disperse heat quickly. 5. Thermal Management in HDI PCB Design Optical module DSPs, optical drivers, and laser diodes generate concentrated heat. High temperatures cause device aging, DK/Df parameter drift, and impedance shifts. Efficient Thermal Paths: Place dense thermal via arrays under high-power devices (DSP, TOSA) to transfer heat from the optical module PCB inner layers to the metal housing. Hot/Cold Component Partitioning: Isolate heat sources from temperature-sensitive optical and clock components to prevent thermal drift and premature aging. Symmetrical Design against Warpage: Balance copper distribution and layer stack-ups across the HDI PCB to manage thermal-mechanical stress during reflow soldering. （Thermal Path IC → Thermal Via → Copper Plane → Housing） 6. EMC and Grounding for High Speed PCB Layout Symmetrical Routing for Common-Mode Noise: Maintain structural symmetry in high-speed differential traces to reduce EMI radiation. Connect the module metal shell to the PCB ground for low-impedance shielding. Interface ESD Protection : Place TVS diodes and common-mode chokes near edge connectors to route ESD currents quickly to chassis ground. Isolate Interference Sources: Keep power inductors and switching regulators away from sensitive RX analog inputs to prevent magnetic coupling. 7. DFM Guidelines for Optical Module PCB Manufacturing Precise HDI pcb design and assembly standards ensure manufacturing yield for dense components. Precision Soldering Design: Use Via-in-Pad or micro-vias for high-density BGAs. For QFN thermal pads, use segmented stencil openings to reduce solder voiding and floating. Optical Alignment Tolerance: Match mechanical outline and mounting hole tolerances precisely with metal housings to avoid optical misalignments. Test Points and Gold Fingers: Keep test points off high-speed trunk lines. Use hard gold plating for edge connector gold fingers to ensure durability across insertion cycles. 8.Optical Module PCB vs Standard PCB Core Differences Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design by: Mila Sep 03,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hdi pcb HDI pcb design optical module pcb high speed pcb layout An optical module PCB is a typical high-frequency, high-density HDI PCB precision board. Its material selection is closely related to transmission rate, link length, loss budget, and device platforms. While 10G and lower modules can use materials like high-Tg FR-4, high-speed modules operating at 25G, 56G, 100G, 400G, and 800G impose stringent requirements on low-loss materials, impedance control, and manufacturing consistency. Below are seven core layout design points and key differences compared to standard PCBs, focusing on high speed pcb layout and practical signal integrity engineering without rigid design fallacies. 1. Substrate Selection and StackUp Design Substrate selection and layer stackup form the foundation for stable high-frequency transmission, directly determining link insertion loss, impedance accuracy, and signal integrity. Multi-Dimensional Rate-Matched Selection: For 25G+ channels, select substrates considering Nyquist frequency, link length, insertion loss budget, dielectric loss, copper foil roughness, and stackup. For long-distance or low-loss channels, choose mid-to-low loss high-speed substrates. Non-critical areas like low-speed control and power can use high-Tg FR-4 to balance performance and cost on an optical module PCB. Adjacent Reference Ground Planes: High-speed differential signal layers should adopt a "signal-reference ground" structure to minimize edge-field coupling. Power layers should pair with adjacent ground layers to optimize PDN impedance via inter-layer capacitance. Pre-Simulation Impedance Modeling: Determine stackup parameters early through SI simulation. The industry standard target is typically 100 ohms differential impedance, with high-performance channels strictly controlling tolerances within +/- 5%. 2. High-Speed Differential TX/RX Signal Integrity High-speed differential signals are the core of data transmission in an optical module PCB. Design should focus on eliminating geometric discontinuities and parasitic interference. Symmetry and Equal Length: Match trace widths, spacing, bends, and via layouts for differential pairs. Advanced HDI pcb design requires controlling intra-pair length skew to prevent differential-to-common mode noise conversion. Trace Geometry Continuity: Use 45-degree angles or smooth arc transitions instead of rigid 90-degree turns. High-frequency reflections stem mostly from vias, pads, stubs, and split reference planes rather than standard trace corners. Minimal Via Structures and Stub Optimization: Minimize layer transitions. For long through-hole structures, apply back-drilling to remove residual stubs, cutting down reflections and resonances. （Backdrill + Via Stub） Unbroken High-Frequency Return Paths: Avoid routing differential traces across ground splits or slot gaps. Provide nearby stitching ground vias whenever signals switch layers. (Differential Pair + Reference Plane + Return Path) Crosstalk Mitigation: Apply the 3W rule during initial layout for proper spacing. For 112G PAM4 ultra-high-speed scenarios, refine trace spacing with 3D EM simulation and add ground via shielding walls where necessary. 3. Optoelectronic Isolation and Sensitive Layout Optical modules combine sensitive analog signals with high-speed digital logic. The analog front-end requires isolation from power and digital noise. Physical Isolation: Separate TOSA/ROSA components and TIA analog circuits from high-speed digital traces and switching power supplies based on form factors (SFP, QSFP, OSFP). Short Analog Traces: Keep weak analog traces from optical devices to TIA and driver ICs as short as possible, avoiding parallel routing alongside high-speed digital lines. Analog Circuit Shielding: Implement localized ground shielding or small metal shields around laser drivers and TIA circuits to isolate high-frequency digital noise. 4. Power Integrity (PI) Optimization Focus on low-impedance return paths, minimal current loops, and sub-region noise reduction. Minimal Loop Decoupling: Configure decoupling networks based on target PDN impedance. Place capacitors close to power pins to minimize parasitic inductance. Solid Ground Plane Priority: Maintain a continuous, low-impedance ground plane across the HDI PCB to provide a solid reference. Apply localized filtering for sensitive analog zones rather than single-point star grounding across the board. Thermal Copper Pour for Power Chips: Place large copper areas with thermal via arrays beneath heat-generating components like laser drivers to disperse heat quickly. 5. Thermal Management in HDI PCB Design Optical module DSPs, optical drivers, and laser diodes generate concentrated heat. High temperatures cause device aging, DK/Df parameter drift, and impedance shifts. Efficient Thermal Paths: Place dense thermal via arrays under high-power devices (DSP, TOSA) to transfer heat from the optical module PCB inner layers to the metal housing. Hot/Cold Component Partitioning: Isolate heat sources from temperature-sensitive optical and clock components to prevent thermal drift and premature aging. Symmetrical Design against Warpage: Balance copper distribution and layer stack-ups across the HDI PCB to manage thermal-mechanical stress during reflow soldering. （Thermal Path IC → Thermal Via → Copper Plane → Housing） 6. EMC and Grounding for High Speed PCB Layout Symmetrical Routing for Common-Mode Noise: Maintain structural symmetry in high-speed differential traces to reduce EMI radiation. Connect the module metal shell to the PCB ground for low-impedance shielding. Interface ESD Protection : Place TVS diodes and common-mode chokes near edge connectors to route ESD currents quickly to chassis ground. Isolate Interference Sources: Keep power inductors and switching regulators away from sensitive RX analog inputs to prevent magnetic coupling. 7. DFM Guidelines for Optical Module PCB Manufacturing Precise HDI pcb design and assembly standards ensure manufacturing yield for dense components. Precision Soldering Design: Use Via-in-Pad or micro-vias for high-density BGAs. For QFN thermal pads, use segmented stencil openings to reduce solder voiding and floating. Optical Alignment Tolerance: Match mechanical outline and mounting hole tolerances precisely with metal housings to avoid optical misalignments. Test Points and Gold Fingers: Keep test points off high-speed trunk lines. Use hard gold plating for edge connector gold fingers to ensure durability across insertion cycles. 8.Optical Module PCB vs Standard PCB Core Differences Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design by: Mila Sep 03,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hdi pcb HDI pcb design optical module pcb high speed pcb layout An optical module PCB is a typical high-frequency, high-density HDI PCB precision board. Its material selection is closely related to transmission rate, link length, loss budget, and device platforms. While 10G and lower modules can use materials like high-Tg FR-4, high-speed modules operating at 25G, 56G, 100G, 400G, and 800G impose stringent requirements on low-loss materials, impedance control, and manufacturing consistency. Below are seven core layout design points and key differences compared to standard PCBs, focusing on high speed pcb layout and practical signal integrity engineering without rigid design fallacies. 1. Substrate Selection and StackUp Design Substrate selection and layer stackup form the foundation for stable high-frequency transmission, directly determining link insertion loss, impedance accuracy, and signal integrity. Multi-Dimensional Rate-Matched Selection: For 25G+ channels, select substrates considering Nyquist frequency, link length, insertion loss budget, dielectric loss, copper foil roughness, and stackup. For long-distance or low-loss channels, choose mid-to-low loss high-speed substrates. Non-critical areas like low-speed control and power can use high-Tg FR-4 to balance performance and cost on an optical module PCB. Adjacent Reference Ground Planes: High-speed differential signal layers should adopt a "signal-reference ground" structure to minimize edge-field coupling. Power layers should pair with adjacent ground layers to optimize PDN impedance via inter-layer capacitance. Pre-Simulation Impedance Modeling: Determine stackup parameters early through SI simulation. The industry standard target is typically 100 ohms differential impedance, with high-performance channels strictly controlling tolerances within +/- 5%. 2. High-Speed Differential TX/RX Signal Integrity High-speed differential signals are the core of data transmission in an optical module PCB. Design should focus on eliminating geometric discontinuities and parasitic interference. Symmetry and Equal Length: Match trace widths, spacing, bends, and via layouts for differential pairs. Advanced HDI pcb design requires controlling intra-pair length skew to prevent differential-to-common mode noise conversion. Trace Geometry Continuity: Use 45-degree angles or smooth arc transitions instead of rigid 90-degree turns. High-frequency reflections stem mostly from vias, pads, stubs, and split reference planes rather than standard trace corners. Minimal Via Structures and Stub Optimization: Minimize layer transitions. For long through-hole structures, apply back-drilling to remove residual stubs, cutting down reflections and resonances. （Backdrill + Via Stub） Unbroken High-Frequency Return Paths: Avoid routing differential traces across ground splits or slot gaps. Provide nearby stitching ground vias whenever signals switch layers. (Differential Pair + Reference Plane + Return Path) Crosstalk Mitigation: Apply the 3W rule during initial layout for proper spacing. For 112G PAM4 ultra-high-speed scenarios, refine trace spacing with 3D EM simulation and add ground via shielding walls where necessary. 3. Optoelectronic Isolation and Sensitive Layout Optical modules combine sensitive analog signals with high-speed digital logic. The analog front-end requires isolation from power and digital noise. Physical Isolation: Separate TOSA/ROSA components and TIA analog circuits from high-speed digital traces and switching power supplies based on form factors (SFP, QSFP, OSFP). Short Analog Traces: Keep weak analog traces from optical devices to TIA and driver ICs as short as possible, avoiding parallel routing alongside high-speed digital lines. Analog Circuit Shielding: Implement localized ground shielding or small metal shields around laser drivers and TIA circuits to isolate high-frequency digital noise. 4. Power Integrity (PI) Optimization Focus on low-impedance return paths, minimal current loops, and sub-region noise reduction. Minimal Loop Decoupling: Configure decoupling networks based on target PDN impedance. Place capacitors close to power pins to minimize parasitic inductance. Solid Ground Plane Priority: Maintain a continuous, low-impedance ground plane across the HDI PCB to provide a solid reference. Apply localized filtering for sensitive analog zones rather than single-point star grounding across the board. Thermal Copper Pour for Power Chips: Place large copper areas with thermal via arrays beneath heat-generating components like laser drivers to disperse heat quickly. 5. Thermal Management in HDI PCB Design Optical module DSPs, optical drivers, and laser diodes generate concentrated heat. High temperatures cause device aging, DK/Df parameter drift, and impedance shifts. Efficient Thermal Paths: Place dense thermal via arrays under high-power devices (DSP, TOSA) to transfer heat from the optical module PCB inner layers to the metal housing. Hot/Cold Component Partitioning: Isolate heat sources from temperature-sensitive optical and clock components to prevent thermal drift and premature aging. Symmetrical Design against Warpage: Balance copper distribution and layer stack-ups across the HDI PCB to manage thermal-mechanical stress during reflow soldering. （Thermal Path IC → Thermal Via → Copper Plane → Housing） 6. EMC and Grounding for High Speed PCB Layout Symmetrical Routing for Common-Mode Noise: Maintain structural symmetry in high-speed differential traces to reduce EMI radiation. Connect the module metal shell to the PCB ground for low-impedance shielding. Interface ESD Protection : Place TVS diodes and common-mode chokes near edge connectors to route ESD currents quickly to chassis ground. Isolate Interference Sources: Keep power inductors and switching regulators away from sensitive RX analog inputs to prevent magnetic coupling. 7. DFM Guidelines for Optical Module PCB Manufacturing Precise HDI pcb design and assembly standards ensure manufacturing yield for dense components. Precision Soldering Design: Use Via-in-Pad or micro-vias for high-density BGAs. For QFN thermal pads, use segmented stencil openings to reduce solder voiding and floating. Optical Alignment Tolerance: Match mechanical outline and mounting hole tolerances precisely with metal housings to avoid optical misalignments. Test Points and Gold Fingers: Keep test points off high-speed trunk lines. Use hard gold plating for edge connector gold fingers to ensure durability across insertion cycles. 8.Optical Module PCB vs Standard PCB Core Differences Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices by: Mila Sep 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout high speed analog to digital converter high speed adc adc layout adc pcb design High-speed analog-to-digital converter (ADC) PCB layout involves multiple design parameters, and their importance varies depending on the application. For high-speed ADC systems, the focus should not be on optimizing every routing detail, but on avoiding common design deviations and maintaining the overall performance of the signal chain. For a broader overview of PCB Layout principles, designers should also consider signal integrity, power integrity, grounding, and return paths as part of the overall design. 1. EPAD Design Guidelines for ADC PCB Design The exposed pad (EPAD), defined as Pin 0 by ADI, is the core pad located on the bottom of many integrated circuit packages. It typically provides the main grounding and thermal connection and serves as an important path for the internal ground structure. Some converters and amplifiers do not have dedicated ground pins, with their grounding function primarily relying on the EPAD. Therefore, EPAD design directly affects electrical connection stability and thermal performance and should not be overlooked in ADC PCB design. The EPAD must form a reliable solder connection with the PCB to ensure both electrical and thermal connectivity. Poor soldering or insufficient contact can lead to abnormal grounding, inadequate heat dissipation, and even malfunction of the signal chain. For reliable EPAD performance, three key aspects should be considered in ADC PCB design. Multilayer Grounding and Thermal Copper According to the device datasheet and overall thermal requirements, grounding and thermal copper structures can be added on the appropriate PCB layers. These structures should provide reliable electrical and thermal connections to the PCB ground planes, helping improve heat dissipation, particularly in high-power and multichannel signal-chain applications. The bottom layer can also incorporate a corresponding grounding or thermal area when required by the device and system design. Depending on the application, this area can support grounding, thermal management, high-frequency decoupling, or mechanical positioning for a bottom-side thermal structure. （exposed pad pcb design） EPAD Pad Segmentation A large EPAD can be divided into multiple smaller areas using a cross-hatched stencil pattern or solder mask segmentation. During reflow soldering, solder paste distribution can vary across a large continuous pad, potentially resulting in uneven soldering, voids, or insufficient effective contact. Proper EPAD segmentation helps improve solder paste distribution and create a more uniform and stable connection between the device and PCB, improving both electrical and thermal reliability. EPAD Ground Vias and Via Filling Ground vias can be added to individual EPAD sections according to the device recommendations and PCB manufacturing requirements. Whether these vias require solder paste filling, epoxy filling, or other treatment depends on the via dimensions, pad structure, and manufacturing process. For via structures that may allow solder paste to flow into the holes during reflow, appropriate via filling or solder mask treatment should be considered. This helps reduce soldering defects and improves the reliability of the EPAD electrical and thermal connection. (EPAD design: large vs segmented) 2. Power Decoupling and PDS Design for High-Speed ADC The primary goal of PCB power decoupling is to reduce the impedance of the power delivery system (PDS) to ground. A common mistake is to place large numbers of capacitors with different capacitance values without considering their actual frequency response. In practice, a large number of redundant capacitors is not always necessary. Carefully selecting capacitors based on capacitance, component type, package, and process characteristics can optimize PDS impedance while saving PCB space and reducing component cost. Redundant capacitors can introduce layout congestion, additional cost, and potential resonance risks. They do not inherently violate PCB manufacturing requirements, but excessive or poorly planned decoupling can reduce overall design efficiency. Capacitor Selection and PCB Decoupling Layout The performance of a capacitor varies with its package and construction. Even capacitors from the same supplier can have different frequency responses depending on package size, process, and component type. Therefore, there is no universal frequency limit for capacitor decoupling performance. The effective frequency range depends on package size, equivalent series inductance (ESL), component characteristics, and the actual PCB layout. If capacitor selection or placement is inappropriate, multiple capacitors can introduce additional inductive loops. Capacitors with different parameters may also resonate at specific frequencies, potentially increasing rather than reducing PDS impedance. Capacitor frequency-response characteristics should therefore be considered before placement and selection. （ADC decoupling capacitor layout） 3. High-Frequency PDS and PCB Stackup Design The effective decoupling range of discrete capacitors depends on their electrical characteristics and PCB layout, and there is no universal high-frequency cutoff. As frequency increases, package parasitics and ESL increasingly limit the high-frequency performance of discrete capacitors. At higher frequencies, the intrinsic capacitance formed between PCB power and ground planes becomes an important part of PDS design. Proper stackup design can therefore complement conventional discrete decoupling. Six-Layer PCB Stackup A typical six-layer PCB stackup can be arranged as: Top Signal → Ground 1 → Power 1 → Power 2 → Ground 2 → Bottom Signal In high-speed PCB design, keeping the dielectric thickness between adjacent power and ground planes relatively small, such as a typical range of 2–4 mil, helps increase plane capacitance and reduce the impedance of high-frequency current paths. This optimization is achieved primarily through the PCB stackup and does not require additional components. The required stackup and dielectric thickness simply need to be specified in the PCB fabrication documentation. Eight-Layer PCB Stackup Optimization For an eight-layer PCB, additional ground reference layers can be introduced while maintaining a small core-layer spacing, such as 2–3 mil. This can significantly increase the intrinsic plane capacitance, although the actual increase is not necessarily double. It depends on dielectric thickness, copper area, and the overall configuration of the power and ground layers. Compared with simply adding more high-frequency discrete capacitors, stackup optimization can reduce component count and provide a cleaner high-frequency PDS structure. PDS Impedance and Dynamic Current The primary function of the PDS is to suppress voltage fluctuations caused by the dynamic current demand of the circuit. Low-impedance power and ground planes, combined with an appropriate PCB stackup, can reduce voltage fluctuations caused by rapidly changing currents. According to V = IR, if the dynamic current is 1 A and the PDS impedance is 10 mΩ, the corresponding voltage variation is approximately 10 mV. Optimizing the PCB stackup can extend the effective high-frequency low-impedance range, but overall PDS performance is also affected by power-plane integrity, ground-via placement, package parasitics, and local current-loop design. Therefore, conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can be placed at key locations such as power-entry points, high-power devices, and surge-current devices. Combining different decoupling mechanisms can help optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. Dense capacitor placement around every IC is not always necessary and may introduce unnecessary cost, space consumption, and resonance risks. （discrete vs plane capacitance） 4. PCB Layer-to-Layer Coupling and Noise Suppression In multilayer PCB layouts, sensitive analog layers, including analog power, ground, and signal layers, can experience crosstalk when placed close to high-frequency digital layers. Because some noise sources are located directly above or below sensitive analog layers, this type of coupling can easily be overlooked. Layer Coupling in ADC Layout Adjacent PCB conductor layers form parasitic capacitive structures, which can produce electric-field coupling under certain frequency and layout conditions. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. Verify Now Blog > High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices by: Mila Sep 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout high speed analog to digital converter high speed adc adc layout adc pcb design High-speed analog-to-digital converter (ADC) PCB layout involves multiple design parameters, and their importance varies depending on the application. For high-speed ADC systems, the focus should not be on optimizing every routing detail, but on avoiding common design deviations and maintaining the overall performance of the signal chain. For a broader overview of PCB Layout principles, designers should also consider signal integrity, power integrity, grounding, and return paths as part of the overall design. 1. EPAD Design Guidelines for ADC PCB Design The exposed pad (EPAD), defined as Pin 0 by ADI, is the core pad located on the bottom of many integrated circuit packages. It typically provides the main grounding and thermal connection and serves as an important path for the internal ground structure. Some converters and amplifiers do not have dedicated ground pins, with their grounding function primarily relying on the EPAD. Therefore, EPAD design directly affects electrical connection stability and thermal performance and should not be overlooked in ADC PCB design. The EPAD must form a reliable solder connection with the PCB to ensure both electrical and thermal connectivity. Poor soldering or insufficient contact can lead to abnormal grounding, inadequate heat dissipation, and even malfunction of the signal chain. For reliable EPAD performance, three key aspects should be considered in ADC PCB design. Multilayer Grounding and Thermal Copper According to the device datasheet and overall thermal requirements, grounding and thermal copper structures can be added on the appropriate PCB layers. These structures should provide reliable electrical and thermal connections to the PCB ground planes, helping improve heat dissipation, particularly in high-power and multichannel signal-chain applications. The bottom layer can also incorporate a corresponding grounding or thermal area when required by the device and system design. Depending on the application, this area can support grounding, thermal management, high-frequency decoupling, or mechanical positioning for a bottom-side thermal structure. （exposed pad pcb design） EPAD Pad Segmentation A large EPAD can be divided into multiple smaller areas using a cross-hatched stencil pattern or solder mask segmentation. During reflow soldering, solder paste distribution can vary across a large continuous pad, potentially resulting in uneven soldering, voids, or insufficient effective contact. Proper EPAD segmentation helps improve solder paste distribution and create a more uniform and stable connection between the device and PCB, improving both electrical and thermal reliability. EPAD Ground Vias and Via Filling Ground vias can be added to individual EPAD sections according to the device recommendations and PCB manufacturing requirements. Whether these vias require solder paste filling, epoxy filling, or other treatment depends on the via dimensions, pad structure, and manufacturing process. For via structures that may allow solder paste to flow into the holes during reflow, appropriate via filling or solder mask treatment should be considered. This helps reduce soldering defects and improves the reliability of the EPAD electrical and thermal connection. (EPAD design: large vs segmented) 2. Power Decoupling and PDS Design for High-Speed ADC The primary goal of PCB power decoupling is to reduce the impedance of the power delivery system (PDS) to ground. A common mistake is to place large numbers of capacitors with different capacitance values without considering their actual frequency response. In practice, a large number of redundant capacitors is not always necessary. Carefully selecting capacitors based on capacitance, component type, package, and process characteristics can optimize PDS impedance while saving PCB space and reducing component cost. Redundant capacitors can introduce layout congestion, additional cost, and potential resonance risks. They do not inherently violate PCB manufacturing requirements, but excessive or poorly planned decoupling can reduce overall design efficiency. Capacitor Selection and PCB Decoupling Layout The performance of a capacitor varies with its package and construction. Even capacitors from the same supplier can have different frequency responses depending on package size, process, and component type. Therefore, there is no universal frequency limit for capacitor decoupling performance. The effective frequency range depends on package size, equivalent series inductance (ESL), component characteristics, and the actual PCB layout. If capacitor selection or placement is inappropriate, multiple capacitors can introduce additional inductive loops. Capacitors with different parameters may also resonate at specific frequencies, potentially increasing rather than reducing PDS impedance. Capacitor frequency-response characteristics should therefore be considered before placement and selection. （ADC decoupling capacitor layout） 3. High-Frequency PDS and PCB Stackup Design The effective decoupling range of discrete capacitors depends on their electrical characteristics and PCB layout, and there is no universal high-frequency cutoff. As frequency increases, package parasitics and ESL increasingly limit the high-frequency performance of discrete capacitors. At higher frequencies, the intrinsic capacitance formed between PCB power and ground planes becomes an important part of PDS design. Proper stackup design can therefore complement conventional discrete decoupling. Six-Layer PCB Stackup A typical six-layer PCB stackup can be arranged as: Top Signal → Ground 1 → Power 1 → Power 2 → Ground 2 → Bottom Signal In high-speed PCB design, keeping the dielectric thickness between adjacent power and ground planes relatively small, such as a typical range of 2–4 mil, helps increase plane capacitance and reduce the impedance of high-frequency current paths. This optimization is achieved primarily through the PCB stackup and does not require additional components. The required stackup and dielectric thickness simply need to be specified in the PCB fabrication documentation. Eight-Layer PCB Stackup Optimization For an eight-layer PCB, additional ground reference layers can be introduced while maintaining a small core-layer spacing, such as 2–3 mil. This can significantly increase the intrinsic plane capacitance, although the actual increase is not necessarily double. It depends on dielectric thickness, copper area, and the overall configuration of the power and ground layers. Compared with simply adding more high-frequency discrete capacitors, stackup optimization can reduce component count and provide a cleaner high-frequency PDS structure. PDS Impedance and Dynamic Current The primary function of the PDS is to suppress voltage fluctuations caused by the dynamic current demand of the circuit. Low-impedance power and ground planes, combined with an appropriate PCB stackup, can reduce voltage fluctuations caused by rapidly changing currents. According to V = IR, if the dynamic current is 1 A and the PDS impedance is 10 mΩ, the corresponding voltage variation is approximately 10 mV. Optimizing the PCB stackup can extend the effective high-frequency low-impedance range, but overall PDS performance is also affected by power-plane integrity, ground-via placement, package parasitics, and local current-loop design. Therefore, conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can be placed at key locations such as power-entry points, high-power devices, and surge-current devices. Combining different decoupling mechanisms can help optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. Dense capacitor placement around every IC is not always necessary and may introduce unnecessary cost, space consumption, and resonance risks. （discrete vs plane capacitance） 4. PCB Layer-to-Layer Coupling and Noise Suppression In multilayer PCB layouts, sensitive analog layers, including analog power, ground, and signal layers, can experience crosstalk when placed close to high-frequency digital layers. Because some noise sources are located directly above or below sensitive analog layers, this type of coupling can easily be overlooked. Layer Coupling in ADC Layout Adjacent PCB conductor layers form parasitic capacitive structures, which can produce electric-field coupling under certain frequency and layout conditions. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. By addressing these factors together, designers can improve the stability and overall performance of high-speed ADC systems. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
